body.working_title: Good practice for evaluating predictions: what the literature supports

body.text: Brief requirements (from the supervisor, 2026-11-13): (1) a claimset based on prediction.md of entrylib/study-planning (v0.2, commit 104ba1c); (2) a pure literature summary: each claim is a statement of good practice supported by the paper(s) it rests on, no new computation; (3) one claim per default and one per Avoid item (supervisor's choice); (4) what not to do is stated as separate claims, with references; (5) papers cited by DOI, captured from open-access copies where they can be reached (supervisor's choice); (6) kept in the lab, on branch claimset/prediction-good-practice of entrylib/study-planning.

Which measures and tests should a study use to evaluate and compare predictions (point forecasts of a mean, a median or a quantile, prediction intervals, predictive distributions, class probabilities), according to the methodological literature on evaluating forecasts and classifiers?

body.definition: A scoring function (an error measure for point forecasts) is consistent for a functional of the predictive distribution, such as the mean, the median or a quantile, when its expected value is lowest when the point forecast equals that functional.

A scoring rule for probabilistic forecasts is proper when its expected value is best when the forecast distribution equals the distribution of the outcome, and strictly proper when it is best only then.
A single-valued forecast meant to equal the mean (expected value) of the outcome's distribution given the information available.
A single-valued forecast meant to equal the median of the outcome's distribution given the information available.
Root mean squared error: the square root of the mean of the squared differences between outcomes and point forecasts.
Root mean squared scaled error: the RMSE of a series' forecasts divided by the in-sample RMSE of the one-step naive forecast of that series, so that series on different scales can be averaged.
Mean absolute error: the mean of the absolute differences between outcomes and point forecasts.
Mean absolute scaled error: the MAE of a series' forecasts divided by the in-sample MAE of the one-step naive forecast of that series.
Mean absolute percentage error: the mean of the absolute differences between outcomes and point forecasts, each divided by the outcome.
Symmetric mean absolute percentage error: the mean of the absolute differences between outcomes and point forecasts, each divided by the mean of the absolute outcome and the absolute forecast.
The beta-median with beta = -1: the point forecast that minimises the expected absolute percentage error; for positive outcomes it lies below the median.
The quantile (asymmetric piecewise linear) loss at level tau: tau times the error when the outcome is above the forecast, and (1 - tau) times the absolute error when it is below.
The score of a central (1 - alpha) prediction interval: its width plus 2/alpha times the distance by which the outcome falls outside it.
The share of outcomes that fall inside the prediction intervals, compared with their nominal level.
Continuous ranked probability score: the integral over thresholds of the squared difference between the forecast's cumulative distribution function and the step function at the outcome.
The logarithmic score: the negative logarithm of the forecast density (or probability) at the outcome.
The mean squared difference between forecast probabilities of a class and the outcome coded 1 if the class occurred and 0 otherwise.
The value of the forecast's cumulative distribution function at the outcome; for a calibrated forecast its values are uniformly distributed.
Statistical consistency between forecast distributions and outcomes: events forecast with a given probability occur with that frequency.
The concentration of the forecast distributions, a property of the forecasts alone; among calibrated forecasts, sharper ones are better.
The share of cases whose predicted class, after thresholding the predicted probabilities, equals the observed class.
The area under the ROC curve: the probability that a randomly chosen case of the positive class receives a higher score than a randomly chosen case of the negative class.
The curve of precision (the share of predicted positives that are positive) against recall (the share of positives predicted as positive) over the classification thresholds.
A time series with many zero values, such as the sales of a slow-moving item.
A non-parametric test of whether several methods differ, applied to their ranks on each of several data sets.
A post-hoc test after the Friedman test that compares every pair of methods by their mean ranks against a critical difference.
Multiple comparisons with the best: a test, on mean ranks over series, of which methods differ significantly from the best-ranked one.
A test of equal expected loss of two competing forecasts of the same series, based on the mean loss differential and its long-run variance.
Correcting a forecast back-transformed from a Box-Cox or log scale so that it estimates the mean, not the median, of the forecast distribution.
Exponential smoothing state space models with error, trend and seasonal components, each additive, multiplicative or absent.

body.statement: To evaluate point forecasts, use a [[TM1:consistent scoring function]] for the functional the forecasts target (the mean, the median or a quantile): a scoring function consistent for a different functional rewards a different forecast from the one the method was built to make.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: TM1
conditions: the functional the forecasts target is known

body.statement: Point forecasts of the mean ([[TM3:point forecast of the mean]]) should be evaluated with squared error ([[TM5:RMSE]]), the scoring function consistent for the mean.
body.question: Q1

body.statement: When [[TM3:point forecasts of the mean]] are compared over series on different scales, the [[TM5:RMSE]] of each series should be scaled by the in-sample RMSE of the one-step naive forecast ([[TM6:RMSSE]]), as the M5 accuracy competition did; scaling each series by a fixed number keeps the comparison consistent for the mean.
body.question: Q1

body.statement: The point forecasts of [[TM30:ETS]] models are [[TM3:point forecasts of the mean]] (conditional means of the forecast distribution), except, beyond one step ahead, for models with a multiplicative trend or multiplicative seasonality.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: TM30
conditions: additive trend and seasonality, or one step ahead

body.statement: Point forecasts made on a Box-Cox or log scale and transformed back to the original scale are [[TM4:point forecasts of the median]], not of the mean, unless they are bias-adjusted ([[TM29:bias adjustment]]).
body.question: Q1

body.statement: [[TM7:MAE]] and [[TM8:MASE]] should not be the main measure for [[TM3:point forecasts of the mean]]: absolute error is consistent for the median and rewards median forecasts.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: TM7
about.relation: should not be the main measure for

body.statement: [[TM9:MAPE]] should not be the measure for point forecasts of the mean or the median: it is consistent for the [[TM11:median of order -1]], which lies below the median for positive outcomes, so it rewards forecasts that are too low.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: TM9
about.relation: should not be the measure for
about.object: point forecasts of the mean or the median

body.statement: [[TM10:sMAPE]] should not be the measure for point forecasts: it penalises errors of the same size differently depending on their sign, and it is undefined when the outcome and the forecast are both zero.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: TM10
about.relation: should not be the measure for

body.statement: Point forecasts of the median ([[TM4:point forecast of the median]]) should be evaluated with absolute error ([[TM7:MAE]]), the scoring function consistent for the median, and, across series on different scales, with [[TM8:MASE]].
body.question: Q1

body.statement: On [[TM24:intermittent series]], absolute-error measures should not be used alone: the median of the outcome can be zero, and absolute error then rewards a forecast of zero for every period.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: absolute-error measures
about.relation: should not be used alone on

body.statement: Quantile forecasts should be evaluated with the [[TM12:pinball loss]] at the quantile's level, the scoring function consistent for that quantile, averaged over the levels when there are several, and scaled per series when series are on different scales.
body.question: Q1

body.statement: Prediction intervals should be evaluated with the [[TM13:interval score]], a proper scoring rule for central intervals, reported together with their [[TM14:coverage]] against the nominal level.
body.question: Q1

body.statement: [[TM14:coverage]] alone should not be the measure of prediction intervals: it does not measure their width, so sharp intervals and needlessly wide ones can reach the same coverage.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: TM14
about.relation: should not be the only measure of

body.statement: Predictive distributions should be evaluated with a [[TM2:proper scoring rule]], such as the [[TM15:CRPS]] or the [[TM16:log score]].
body.question: Q1

body.statement: The evaluation of predictive distributions should check their [[TM19:calibration]], with the [[TM18:probability integral transform]] or coverage at several levels, and report their [[TM20:sharpness]]: the goal is the sharpest forecast that is calibrated.
body.question: Q1

body.statement: Predictive distributions of counts, such as forecasts of intermittent sales, should be evaluated with proper scoring rules and a randomised [[TM18:probability integral transform]], since the probability integral transform of a discrete forecast is not uniform even when the forecast is calibrated.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: proper scoring rules and the randomised PIT

body.statement: Forecast probabilities of classes should be evaluated with a [[TM2:proper scoring rule]], such as the [[TM16:log score]] or the [[TM17:Brier score]].
body.question: Q1

body.statement: [[TM21:accuracy]] should not be the measure of forecast class probabilities: it ignores the probabilities beyond which side of a threshold they fall, and weighs every error the same.
body.question: Q1

body.statement: [[TM22:AUC]] should not be the measure of forecast class probabilities: it measures how well cases are ranked, not whether the probabilities are right, and it weighs the costs of misclassification differently for different classifiers.
body.question: Q1

about.relation: should not be the measure of

body.statement: With rare positive cases, the [[TM23:precision-recall curve]] should be reported rather than the ROC curve alone, because the ROC curve can look good while most cases predicted positive are negative.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: TM23
about.relation: is more informative than the ROC curve for

body.statement: When the compared methods target different functionals (one the mean, another the median), each should be evaluated with a measure consistent for its own target, or the methods made to target the same functional, because a single measure favours the methods that target what it is consistent for.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: the comparison of methods with different targets

body.statement: When methods are compared over many series or data sets, the distribution of their scaled errors across the series should be reported, not only the mean, because a mean over data sets is sensitive to a few outlying ones.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: the distribution of scaled errors across series

body.statement: When several methods are compared over many data sets, their differences should be tested with the [[TM25:Friedman test]] on ranks followed by [[TM26:Nemenyi test]] post-hoc comparisons, which do not assume the errors are comparable across data sets.
body.question: Q1

body.statement: When the question is which methods differ from the best one over many series, multiple comparisons with the best ([[TM27:MCB]]) on ranks answer it, as in the statistical analysis of the M3 competition.
body.question: Q1

body.statement: The accuracy of two forecasts of the same series should be compared with the [[TM28:Diebold-Mariano test]], which allows forecast errors that are serially correlated and not normally distributed.
body.question: Q1

body.statement: An error measure should not be chosen because a competition or a well-known study used it: the measure has to be consistent for what the compared methods predict.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: the choice of an error measure by precedent

body.text: Kolassa, S. (2020). Why the 'best' point forecast depends on the error or accuracy measure. International Journal of Forecasting 36(1), 208-211, doi:10.1016/j.ijforecast.2019.02.017. Full text not reachable from this session (publisher not allowed); checked on 2026-11-13 by its bibliographic record and abstract: a commentary on the M4 competition arguing that there is no single best point forecast, since different error measures are minimised in expectation by different summaries of the same predictive density, and recommending that competitions accept one point forecast per measure.

Makridakis, S., Spiliotis, E., and Assimakopoulos, V. (2022). M5 accuracy competition: results, findings, and conclusions. International Journal of Forecasting 38(4), 1346-1364, doi:10.1016/j.ijforecast.2021.11.013. Full text not reachable from this session; checked on 2026-11-13 by its bibliographic record and secondary accounts: the competition ranked point forecasts by the weighted RMSSE, the RMSE of each series scaled by the in-sample RMSE of the one-step naive forecast, and chose a squared-error measure because absolute-error measures, optimal for the median, would favour forecasts close to zero on its intermittent series. The reason was read in secondary accounts, not in the paper.

Makridakis, S., Spiliotis, E., Assimakopoulos, V., Chen, Z., Gaba, A., Tsetlin, I., and Winkler, R. L. (2022). The M5 uncertainty competition: results, findings and conclusions. International Journal of Forecasting 38(4), 1365-1385, doi:10.1016/j.ijforecast.2021.10.009. Full text not reachable from this session; checked on 2026-11-13 by its bibliographic record and secondary accounts: participants submitted nine quantiles, scored with a weighted scaled pinball loss.

Goodwin, P., and Lawton, R. (1999). On the asymmetry of the symmetric MAPE. International Journal of Forecasting 15(4), 405-408, doi:10.1016/S0169-2070(99)00007-2. Full text not reachable from this session; checked on 2026-11-13 by its abstract: the sMAPE is far from symmetric in its treatment of positive and negative errors of the same size.

Kolassa, S. (2016). Evaluating predictive count data distributions in retail sales forecasting. International Journal of Forecasting 32(3), 788-803, doi:10.1016/j.ijforecast.2015.12.004. Full text not reachable from this session; checked on 2026-11-13 by its abstract and the author's slides: on intermittent count data, absolute-error measures (MAD, MASE) are minimised by a forecast of zero and so are unsuitable; predictive count distributions are evaluated with proper scoring rules and a randomised probability integral transform.

Brier, G. W. (1950). Verification of forecasts expressed in terms of probability. Monthly Weather Review 78(1), 1-3, doi:10.1175/1520-0493(1950)078<0001:VOFEIT>2.0.CO;2. The publisher refused this session's request; checked on 2026-11-13 by its bibliographic record and later accounts: it defines the score now named after Brier and shows that a forecaster cannot improve its expected value by forecasting other than the probabilities they believe.

Hand, D. J. (2009). Measuring classifier performance: a coherent alternative to the area under the ROC curve. Machine Learning 77(1), 103-123, doi:10.1007/s10994-009-5119-5. Full text not open to this session; checked on 2026-11-13 by its abstract: the AUC is equivalent to averaging the misclassification loss over a cost distribution that depends on the classifier itself, so different classifiers are measured with different cost distributions, which is incoherent; the H measure fixes the cost distribution.

Koning, A. J., Franses, P. H., Hibon, M., and Stekler, H. O. (2005). The M3 competition: statistical tests of the results. International Journal of Forecasting 21(3), 397-409, doi:10.1016/j.ijforecast.2004.10.003. Full text not reachable from this session; checked on 2026-11-13 by its abstract: it applies non-parametric multiple comparisons to the M3 results, analysis of means and multiple comparisons with the best (MCB) on ranks over series.

Diebold, F. X., and Mariano, R. S. (1995). Comparing predictive accuracy. Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 13(3), 253-263, doi:10.1080/07350015.1995.10524599. The NBER working paper (t0169) was reached but is a scan without text; checked on 2026-11-13 by the abstract: it proposes tests of the null hypothesis of no difference in the accuracy of two competing forecasts, allowing loss functions that need not be quadratic and forecast errors that are non-Gaussian, non-zero-mean, serially correlated and contemporaneously correlated.

No paper among those the guide cites is the source for avoiding accuracy as the measure of class probabilities. The claim rests on an argument from the definition of accuracy: it uses a probability only through which side of a threshold it falls, and counts every misclassification as the same loss, so it cannot reward right probabilities or reflect unequal costs.

body.rationale: Gneiting (2011, abstract, SR1): 'If the forecaster receives a directive in the form of a functional, it is critical that the scoring function be consistent for it'; consistency is defined in Section 2.2. Kolassa (2020, NT2) argues from the M4 measures that different error measures are minimised by different summaries of one predictive density.

Gneiting (2011, SR1): 'the squared error scoring function is consistent for the mean' (Section 5, Discussion); the scoring functions consistent for the mean are the Bregman functions (Theorem 3.1, Savage), of which squared error is one.

The M5 accuracy competition (NT3) ranked point forecasts by the RMSSE: the RMSE of each series scaled by the in-sample RMSE of the one-step naive forecast. Dividing a series' squared errors by a fixed positive number does not change which forecast minimises their expected value, so the scaled measure stays consistent for the mean (SR1: squared error is consistent for the mean, Section 5).

Hyndman and Khandakar (2008, SR5, Section 2.2): for many models the conditional means are identical to the point forecasts; 'However, for other models (those with multiplicative trend or multiplicative seasonality), the conditional mean and the point forecast will differ slightly for h ≥ 2.'

Hyndman and Athanasopoulos (2018, SR6, Section 3.2): 'the back-transformed point forecast will not be the mean of the forecast distribution. In fact, it will usually be the median of the forecast distribution (assuming that the distribution on the transformed space is symmetric)'; using the mean instead is called bias adjustment.
Gneiting (2011, SR1, Section 5): squared error is consistent for the mean, 'and the absolute error scoring function for the median'; MASE is a scaled absolute error, so it targets the median too.

Gneiting (2011, SR1, Section 5): the absolute percentage error 'is consistent for a non-standard functional, namely, the median of order −1', which tends to support 'severe underforecasts, as compared to the mean or median'; the beta-median is defined in Section 2.4.

Hyndman and Koehler (2006, SR7, Section 2): the 'symmetric' measures 'are not as symmetric as their name suggests': for the same outcome, sMAPE 'has a heavier penalty when forecasts are low compared to when forecasts are high', and 'the sMAPE can take negative values'; Goodwin and Lawton (1999, NT5) show the asymmetry. With outcome and forecast both zero, its denominator is zero, so it is undefined.

Gneiting (2011, SR1, Section 5): 'the absolute error scoring function' is consistent 'for the median'. Hyndman and Koehler (2006, SR7, abstract): 'we propose that the mean absolute scaled error become the standard measure for comparing forecast accuracy across multiple time series'.

Kolassa (2016, NT6): on intermittent count data, absolute-error measures are minimised by a forecast of zero and are unsuitable. The M5 accuracy competition (NT3) chose a squared-error measure for this reason (read in secondary accounts).

Gneiting (2011, SR1, abstract and Theorem 3.3): a scoring function 'is consistent for a quantile if and only if it is generalized piecewise linear'; the pinball loss is the generalized piecewise linear function of order tau with g(x) = x. The M5 uncertainty competition (NT4) scored nine quantiles with a weighted scaled pinball loss.

Gneiting and Raftery (2007, SR2, Section 1 and Section 6.2): they 'discuss the interval score, a scoring rule for prediction intervals that is proper' for central (1 - alpha) intervals, and propose it as a score 'that addresses width as well as coverage' (abstract).

Gneiting and Raftery (2007, SR2, abstract) propose the interval score because it 'addresses width as well as coverage': coverage alone does not measure width, so a needlessly wide interval can reach the nominal coverage.

Gneiting and Raftery (2007, SR2): 'The CRPS is proper relative to the class P' (Section 4.2) and 'The logarithmic score is strictly proper' (Section 4.1); a proper scoring rule is best in expectation when the forecast distribution is the distribution of the outcome (Section 2).

Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery (2007, SR3, abstract): evaluation 'based on the paradigm of maximizing the sharpness of the predictive distributions subject to calibration', with the probability integral transform histogram as a check of calibration (Section 3).

Kolassa (2016, NT6): predictive distributions of count data are evaluated with proper scoring rules and a randomised probability integral transform, since the probability integral transform of a discrete distribution is not uniform.

Gneiting and Raftery (2007, SR2, Section 3, Example 1, 'Quadratic or Brier score', and the logarithmic score): both are strictly proper for categorical forecasts. Brier (1950, NT7) introduced the score.

The argument of NT11: accuracy uses a probability only through which side of a threshold it falls and counts every error as the same loss, so it cannot reward right probabilities or unequal costs. No cited paper is the source of this claim.

Hand (2009, NT8): the AUC averages the misclassification loss over a cost distribution that depends on the classifier, so it measures different classifiers with different cost distributions; and it is a measure of how cases are ranked, unchanged by any monotone transformation of the scores.

Saito and Rehmsmeier (2015, SR8, title and abstract): 'The Precision-Recall Plot Is More Informative than the ROC Plot When Evaluating Binary Classifiers on Imbalanced Datasets'; the interpretability of ROC plots on imbalanced data 'can be deceptive'.

Kolassa (2020, NT2): different error measures are minimised by different summaries of the same predictive density, so no single point forecast is best for all. Gneiting (2011, SR1, Section 5): squared error is consistent for the mean and absolute error for the median.

Demsar (2006, SR4, Section 3.1): 'Averages are also susceptible to outliers. They allow classifier's excellent performance on one data set to compensate for the overall bad performance, or the opposite'.

Demsar (2006, SR4, abstract): 'we recommend a set of simple, yet safe and robust non-parametric tests', 'the Friedman test with the corresponding post-hoc tests for comparison of more classifiers over multiple data sets', with the Nemenyi test for all pairwise comparisons (Section 3.2.2); averages over data sets may not be commensurable (Section 3.1).
Koning et al. (2005, NT9) test the M3 results with non-parametric multiple comparisons on ranks over series, including multiple comparisons with the best (MCB).

Diebold and Mariano (1995, NT10) propose tests of no difference in the accuracy of two competing forecasts that allow non-quadratic loss and forecast errors that are non-Gaussian, non-zero-mean and serially correlated.

Kolassa (2020, NT2), a commentary on the measures of the M4 competition: the best point forecast depends on the error measure, since each measure is minimised by a different summary of the predictive density. Gneiting (2011, SR1, abstract): it is critical that the scoring function be consistent for the functional the forecasts target.

Gneiting (2011, SR1, Section 5): the absolute percentage error 'is consistent for a non-standard functional, namely, the median of order −1', which tends to support 'severe underforecasts, as compared to the mean or median'; the beta-median is defined in Section 1.3 and the absolute percentage error is shown to be its beta = -1 case in Section 2.3. (Corrects the section named in ST7.)

body.text: The supervisor left the implementation facts out of the study: 'Implementation facts are not needed here. This is a side thing, which belongs to ETS, not this study.' (Ivan Svetunkov, chat, 2026-11-13). H4 (ETS point forecasts are conditional means except with multiplicative trend or seasonality beyond one step) and H5 (back-transformed forecasts are medians unless bias-adjusted) are abandoned as out of scope; they stay in the record with their evidence.

body.statement: [[TM10:sMAPE]] should not be the measure for point forecasts: for the same outcome it penalises forecasts below the outcome more heavily than forecasts above it, so it rewards forecasts that are too high, and it is undefined when the outcome and the forecast are both zero.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: TM10

body.statement: Scale-dependent error measures ([[TM5:RMSE]], [[TM7:MAE]]) should not be summed or averaged across series on different scales: the series with the largest values then dominate the aggregate, whatever the forecasts of the other series.
body.question: Q1

body.statement: To aggregate the accuracy of point forecasts over series on different scales, each series' errors should first be scaled by a quantity of that series (as in [[TM8:MASE]] and [[TM6:RMSSE]], or relative to a benchmark method), and the scaled errors then averaged, choosing a scaling that keeps the measure consistent for what the forecasts target.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: scaling per series before aggregation
about.object: accuracy over series on different scales

body.text: Athanasopoulos, G., and Kourentzes, N. (2023). On the evaluation of hierarchical forecasts. International Journal of Forecasting 39(4), 1502-1511, doi:10.1016/j.ijforecast.2022.08.003 (Monash EBS working paper 10/21, pointed to by the supervisor). Full text not reachable from this session: the Monash pages answer automated requests with a bot challenge; checked on 2026-11-13 by its bibliographic record and abstract: it discusses the scale and units of the time series, intermittency, the forecast horizon, multiple evaluation windows and the decision context as issues in evaluating hierarchical forecasts, and ends with practical recommendations.

body.rationale: Hyndman and Koehler (2006, SR7, Section 2.2): for the same outcome, sMAPE 'has a heavier penalty when forecasts are low compared to when forecasts are high', so of two forecasts the same distance from the outcome the higher one scores better, and 'the sMAPE can take negative values'; Goodwin and Lawton (1999, NT5) show the asymmetry. With outcome and forecast both zero, its denominator is zero, so it is undefined. (H27 corrects H8, whose statement did not say in which direction sMAPE errs.)

Hyndman and Koehler (2006, SR7, Section 2.1): scale-dependent measures 'are useful when comparing different methods on the same set of data, but should not be used, for example, when comparing across data sets that have different scales', and 'It makes no sense to compute the MAE across series (due to their different scales)' (Section 2.3). Athanasopoulos and Kourentzes (2023, NT12) treat the scale and units of the series as an issue in evaluating hierarchical forecasts.

Hyndman and Koehler (2006, SR7, Section 3): 'measures based on scaled errors should become the standard approach in comparing forecast accuracy across series on different scales'; the M5 accuracy competition (NT3) scaled each series' RMSE by its in-sample one-step naive RMSE before averaging. Scaling by a quantity of the series that does not depend on the forecast keeps the measure consistent for what it targets (SR1, squared error for the mean, absolute error for the median).

Hyndman and Koehler (2006, SR7, Section 2.1): scale-dependent measures 'are useful when comparing different methods on the same set of data, but should not be used, for example, when comparing across data sets that have different scales', and 'It makes no sense to compute the MAE across series (due to their different scales)' (Section 2.4). Athanasopoulos and Kourentzes (2023, NT12) treat the scale and units of the series as an issue in evaluating hierarchical forecasts. (Corrects the section named in ST31.)

body.rationale: The M5 Competitors' Guide (SR9, Point forecasts): the RMSSE divides each series' squared errors by the in-sample mean squared error of the one-step naive forecast; 'the accuracy measure used builds on squared errors, which are optimized for the mean', and 'The measure is scale independent, meaning that it can be effectively used to compare forecasts across series with different scales'. (Adds the guide, a primary source, to ST3.)

The M5 Competitors' Guide (SR9, Point forecasts): on intermittent series 'absolute errors, which are optimized for the median, would assign lower scores (better performance) to forecasting methods that derive forecasts close to zero', so M5 used squared errors. Kolassa (2016, NT6) makes the same point for count data. (Replaces the secondary account of ST10 with the primary source.)

Gneiting (2011, SR1, abstract and Theorem 3.3): a scoring function 'is consistent for a quantile if and only if it is generalized piecewise linear'; the pinball loss is the generalized piecewise linear function of order tau with g(x) = x.

The M5 Competitors' Guide (SR9, Probabilistic forecasts): forecasts of quantiles are evaluated with the 'Scaled Pinball Loss (SPL)', the pinball loss of each series and quantile divided by the in-sample mean absolute error of the one-step naive forecast, computed per series; the M5 uncertainty paper (NT4) reports the competition scored this way.

The M4 competition (NT13) evaluated prediction intervals with the mean scaled interval score, the interval score of Gneiting and Raftery (2007, SR2, Section 6.2) scaled per series; a score in the units of the data is scale-dependent and should not be compared across series on different scales (Hyndman and Koehler 2006, SR7, Section 2.1).

Demsar (2006, SR4, Section 3.1): 'Averages are also susceptible to outliers'. Hyndman and Koehler (2006, SR7, Section 3) summarise scaled errors across series; the M5 guide (SR9) averages the RMSSE over the series. The median and quartiles describe the distribution that the mean alone hides.

Demsar (2006, SR4, abstract; Sections 3.1 and 3.2.2): it recommends 'the Friedman test with the corresponding post-hoc tests for comparison of more classifiers over multiple data sets' to test whether observed differences are significant, with the Nemenyi test for all pairs; ranks do not assume that results on different data sets are commensurable.
Koning et al. (2005, NT9) test the M3 results with multiple comparisons with the best (MCB) on ranks over series, which tells which methods differ significantly from the best one.

Hyndman and Koehler (2006, SR7, Section 3): 'measures based on scaled errors should become the standard approach in comparing forecast accuracy across series on different scales'. The M5 guide (SR9) scales each series' errors by its in-sample naive error before averaging, so that the measure 'can be effectively used to compare forecasts across series with different scales'. (Adds the guide to ST32.)
